before.text: Does the agent implement universal service accessibility per EU Web Accessibility Directive 2016/2102 Article 4 and WCAG 2.1 AA success criteria for all citizen-facing service channels?
before.regulatoryRef: EU Accessibility Directive 2016/2102 Art. 4; WCAG 2.1 AA
before.l1: No accessibility compliance; citizen service AI is inaccessible to persons with disabilities, lacks WCAG 2.1 AA conformance, and provides no alternative access channels
before.l3: Agent implements WCAG 2.1 AA for primary service interfaces, but does not apply accessibility to all channels or maintain accessibility statements per Art. 7
before.l5: Full accessibility with WCAG 2.1 AA+ implementation, EU Accessibility Directive Art. 4 compliance, multi-channel service delivery (web, mobile, telephone, in-person), accessibility feedback mechanism, annual accessibility statement per Art. 7, and ATAG 2.0 authoring tool compliance

after.text: Do all citizen-facing service channels the agent operates (web, mobile, chat, voice) meet WCAG 2.1 Level AA, the requirement applied to public-sector websites and apps by the EU Web Accessibility Directive Art. 4, with keyboard focus order (WCAG SC 2.4.3) covered by regression tests and an accessibility statement per Art. 7?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Web Accessibility Directive Art. 4, Art. 7; WCAG 2.1 AA; WCAG 2.2
after.l1: No conformance testing; at least one channel has known blocking accessibility failures
after.l3: Primary web interfaces conform to WCAG 2.1 AA, but other channels or dynamic agent-generated content are untested, or no accessibility statement is published
after.l5: Conformance evidence per release for every channel including agent-generated content; SC 2.4.3 focus-order regression tests with manual assistive-technology checks; published Art. 7 statement with a feedback route; WCAG 2.2 conformance tracked for authentication steps

citations.before: EU Accessibility Directive 2016/2102 Art. 4; WCAG 2.1 AA
citations.after: EU Web Accessibility Directive Art. 4, Art. 7; WCAG 2.1 AA; WCAG 2.2

before.text: For all SDG-scoped procedures, does the agent ensure the full procedure is available fully online end-to-end (including identification/authentication, guidance, form completion, evidence submission, e-signature where applicable, fee/payment, status tracking, decision delivery, and appeal/redress initiation), with documented exceptions and accessibility-preserving alternative channels, per SDG Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 Article 2(2)?
before.l1: Procedure is not fully online: one or more mandatory steps require in-person/phone/mail workarounds or manual staff intervention, with no exception governance or evidence
before.l3: Most steps are online, but identity/evidence/payment/decision delivery or redress steps still require offline actions or are inconsistently available across procedures
before.l5: All SDG procedures are end-to-end fully online with exception governance, evidence of completion rates, cross-border accessibility checks, and auditable proof that offline steps are not mandatory except where legally justified

after.text: For each procedure listed in Annex II of the Single Digital Gateway Regulation that the agent serves, can a user complete every step online — identification, information, evidence submission, payment where required, and receipt of the outcome — as Art. 6(1) requires, with any offline step justified in a documented exception?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Single Digital Gateway Regulation Art. 6(1), Annex II (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724, Art. 6 applies from 12 Dec 2023)
after.l1: One or more mandatory steps of an Annex II procedure require offline action with no documented exception
after.l3: Most steps are online, but identification, evidence, payment or outcome delivery still require offline action for some procedures
after.l5: Every Annex II procedure served is completable online end to end, exceptions are documented with their legal basis, and completion rates are measured per procedure including cross-border users

citations.after: EU Single Digital Gateway Regulation Art. 6(1), Annex II (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724, Art. 6 applies from 12 Dec 2023)

before.text: Does the agent support eIDAS 2.0 cross-border use (per §6) by enabling (1) cross-border identification/authentication acceptance, (2) EUDI Wallet or equivalent credential presentation flows where applicable, (3) relying-party verification and attribute validation, (4) multilingual/cross-border error handling and support, and (5) evidence exports demonstrating successful cross-border transactions and interoperability testing?
before.l1: No cross-border support: identity/credential flows work only for domestic users and fail for cross-border credentials or foreign-issued attributes
before.l3: Some cross-border scenarios work, but coverage is incomplete, usability is poor, and there is limited evidence of interoperability testing and relying-party validation
before.l5: Full cross-border readiness with interoperable identity/credential acceptance, relying-party verification, consistent UX across Member States, and audit-ready evidence of cross-border transactions and conformance testing

after.text: Where a public service the agent fronts requires electronic identification, does it accept EU Digital Identity Wallets and notified eID means from other Member States (eIDAS Art. 5f cross-border reliance on wallets; Art. 6 mutual recognition), with relying-party verification of presented attributes and evidence of cross-border test transactions?
after.l1: Only domestic credentials are accepted
after.l3: Some cross-border credentials work, but wallet acceptance or attribute verification is incomplete, or no cross-border test evidence exists
after.l5: Wallets and notified foreign eID means accepted at the required assurance level, attributes verified, cross-border test transactions recorded per release, and failures handled with multilingual guidance

before.text: Across all citizen-service user journeys (including AI-assisted decision notices, identity steps, uploads, and payments), does the agent ensure WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.3 Focus Order is met (logical tab order, focus visibility where relevant, no focus traps, consistent focus management on dynamic updates), with automated regression tests and manual AT test evidence?
before.l1: No focus-order control: keyboard navigation order is illogical, dynamic steps trap focus, or assistive technology users cannot complete procedures
before.l3: Some pages meet focus order, but complex journeys (wizards/modals/dynamic forms) have inconsistent focus management and limited test evidence
before.l5: End-to-end focus-order compliance across all journeys with automated checks, AT-supported manual test evidence, and change-control gates preventing regressions

before.text: For web-based citizen services, does the agent meet Section 508 Revised Standards (36 CFR Part 1194 Appendices A and C) requirements (including text alternatives, keyboard access, non-interference with assistive tech, form label/field associations, timing control, and accessible documentation), and produce evidence bundles (test reports, exception logs, remediation tracking) suitable for procurement/audit?
before.regulatoryRef: Section 508 Revised Standards (36 CFR Part 1194 Appendices A and C)
before.l1: No 508 mapping: accessibility is asserted but not evidenced against Revised 508 Standards, with gaps in forms/keyboard/AT compatibility
before.l3: Partial mapping: some criteria are met and tested, but gaps remain and evidence is not consistently retained or auditable
before.l5: Full Revised 508 Standards compliance with traceable criteria mapping, repeatable testing, remediation SLAs, and audit-ready evidence bundles

after.text: Do US channels the agent operates meet the applicable federal accessibility rule — for federal agencies, the Revised Section 508 Standards (36 CFR part 1194, Appendix A E205.4: WCAG 2.0 Level A and AA), and for state and local governments, the ADA Title II web and mobile rule (28 CFR part 35) by its extended compliance dates (26 Apr 2027 for populations of 50,000 or more; 26 Apr 2028 otherwise)?
after.regulatoryRef: Section 508 (36 CFR Part 1194, Appendix A E205.4); 28 CFR Part 35 (ADA Title II web and mobile rule as extended by 91 FR 20902)
after.l1: No conformance testing, or the retired §1194.22 is still the reference
after.l3: Automated checks only, or agent-generated dynamic content and authentication steps are untested
after.l5: Conformance evidence per release covering agent-generated content and authentication steps, an exceptions log, and remediation tracked against the applicable compliance date

citations.before: Section 508 Revised Standards (36 CFR Part 1194 Appendices A and C)
citations.after: Section 508 (36 CFR Part 1194, Appendix A E205.4); 28 CFR Part 35 (ADA Title II web and mobile rule as extended by 91 FR 20902)

before.text: For procedures in scope of the Single Digital Gateway Regulation (EU) 2018/1724, does the agent support the Article 14 once-only technical system, retrieving evidence directly from competent authorities at the user's explicit request and letting the user preview it before use?
before.l1: Citizens must upload evidence that authorities already hold
before.l3: Some evidence types are retrieved through the once-only system, but preview and explicit request are not enforced
before.l5: All available evidence types retrieved through the once-only technical system on explicit request, with preview before use, and logged exchanges

after.text: For Single Digital Gateway procedures that need evidence held by another Member State's authority, can the user ask the agent to obtain it through the once-only technical system (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 Art. 14, applicable from 12 Dec 2023), preview it before it is used, and decline its use?
after.regulatoryRef: EU Single Digital Gateway Regulation Art. 14 (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724)
after.l1: Users must obtain and upload cross-border evidence themselves
after.l3: Evidence can be fetched through the once-only system, but the user cannot preview it or decline its use
after.l5: Evidence requested only on explicit user request, previewed by the user before use, use declinable, and each exchange logged

citations.after: EU Single Digital Gateway Regulation Art. 14 (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724)

before.text: Where the agent supports decisions on eligibility for public assistance benefits and services (EU AI Act Annex III point 5(a)), does the authority inform each applicant that a high-risk AI system is being used, as Article 26(11) requires?
before.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Annex III §5(a); EU AI Act Art. 26(11)
before.l1: Applicants are not told that AI is involved in eligibility decisions
before.l3: A general statement exists on the website, not in the applicant's own case
before.l5: Notice given in each case before the decision, stating the system's purpose and the right to an explanation, with the notice recorded on the case file

after.text: Where the agent supports decisions on eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services (EU AI Act Annex III point 5(a)), does the deploying authority inform each affected person that a high-risk AI system is used in the decision about them (Art. 26(11))?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 26(11), Annex III point 5(a)
after.l1: Applicants are not told that a high-risk AI system is used in their case
after.l3: A general statement exists (for example on the website), but notice is not given in each applicant's own case or is not recorded
after.l5: Notice is given in each case before the decision and recorded on the case file, and a periodic sample checks the notice records

citations.before: EU AI Act Annex III §5(a); EU AI Act Art. 26(11)
citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 26(11), Annex III point 5(a)

after.text: When a person affected by an eligibility decision taken on the basis of the agent's output asks for an explanation, can the deploying authority give a clear and meaningful explanation of the AI system's role in the procedure and of the main elements of the decision, built from records kept at decision time (EU AI Act Art. 86(1))?
after.l1: There is no route to request an explanation, or none can be given
after.l3: Explanations are given on request, but they are generic and not built from the specific decision record
after.l5: A published request route, explanations generated from the logged decision trace and reviewed by a named official, and requests and response times logged

before.text: Does the agent implement EU Single Digital Gateway Regulation 2018/1724 Article 6 quality criteria for online procedures and Article 12 user feedback requirements?
before.l1: No EU SDG compliance; digital service delivery does not meet Art. 6 quality criteria including completeness, accuracy, and cross-border accessibility
before.l3: Agent implements core EU SDG Art. 6 quality requirements, but does not maintain Art. 12 user experience statistics or cross-border service integration
before.l5: Full EU SDG compliance with Art. 6 quality criteria for all procedures, cross-border service delivery per Art. 5, Art. 12 user feedback system, quality statistics reporting to European Commission, and Your Europe portal integration

after.text: For procedures linked to the Single Digital Gateway, does the agent let users give feedback on the service they used and pass that feedback into the gateway's user-feedback tool (Regulation (EU) 2018/1724 Art. 25), with the feedback used to fix reported problems?

after.l1: No user-feedback route on SDG-linked procedures
after.l3: Feedback is collected but not passed to the gateway tool, or not linked to fixes
after.l5: Feedback offered at the end of each procedure, forwarded to the gateway tool, and each recurring issue linked to a tracked fix

before.text: Does the agent implement non-discrimination per EU AI Act high-risk requirements for AI systems used in essential government services including benefits administration?
before.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 10, 14; ECHR Art. 14
before.l1: No non-discrimination controls; AI eligibility assessments may discriminate based on protected characteristics without detection or monitoring
before.l3: Agent performs periodic bias audits for service AI and implements basic fairness constraints, but does not maintain EU AI Act Art. 10 data governance requirements or continuous discrimination monitoring
before.l5: Full non-discrimination governance with EU AI Act Art. 10 training data requirements, continuous disparate impact monitoring per ECHR Art. 14, automated adverse outcome investigation, non-discrimination impact assessment for new service AI, and transparent fairness reporting

after.text: Where the agent supports eligibility decisions in essential public services, are training, validation and test data examined for biases likely to affect fundamental rights or lead to discrimination (EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f)), with outcome disparities across protected groups monitored in operation and investigated when they appear?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Art. 10(5) deleted); ECHR Art. 14
after.l1: No bias examination of data and no outcome monitoring
after.l3: Data were examined for bias before deployment, but outcomes are not monitored by group in operation, or disparities are not investigated
after.l5: Documented Art. 10(2)(f) examination per dataset version, outcome disparities monitored by group in production with thresholds, each breach investigated and its resolution recorded, and results reported to the oversight body

citations.before: EU AI Act Art. 10, 14; ECHR Art. 14
citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 10(2)(f) as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 (Art. 10(5) deleted); ECHR Art. 14

before.text: Does the agent implement EU AI Act Article 14 human oversight for high-risk AI in essential public services and Article 13 transparency for citizens receiving AI-influenced decisions?
before.l1: No human oversight or citizen transparency; AI-influenced government service decisions are made without citizen notification or accessible human review mechanism
before.l3: Agent implements human review capability for flagged AI decisions, but does not provide Art. 13 citizen transparency or systematic human oversight per Art. 14 requirements
before.l5: Full EU AI Act compliance with Art. 13 citizen notification of AI involvement, Art. 14 human oversight with meaningful review capability, citizen explanation of AI-influenced decisions, contestability mechanisms, and national competent authority system registration

after.text: For high-risk agents in essential public services, has the deploying authority assigned human oversight to named people with the competence, training and authority to do it (EU AI Act Art. 26(2)), and can those people disregard, override or reverse the agent's output and stop it safely (Art. 14(4)(d)-(e))?
after.l1: No named overseer, or overseers cannot override or stop the agent
after.l3: Overseers are named and can override outputs, but there is no safe stop, or training and authority are not documented
after.l5: Named overseers with recorded training and authority; override, reversal and stop functions tested each release; every override logged with a reason and reviewed

before.text: Does the agent implement proportionate data use per GDPR Article 6(1)(e) public task processing limitation and Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation for citizen service AI systems?

after.text: Does the agent implement proportionate data use per GDPR Article 6(1)(e) public task processing limitation and Article 5(1)(b) purpose limitation for citizen service AI systems?

after.l5: Full proportionate data governance with GDPR Art. 6(1)(e) necessity assessment for each service AI, Art. 5(1)(b) purpose limitation technical controls, cross-agency data sharing proportionality gates, citizen data transparency dashboards, and automated retention enforcement

before.text: Does the agent implement proactive identification of vulnerable citizen populations per EU AI Act recitals 47-49 and UN SDG 10 Reduced Inequalities to prevent service exclusion?
before.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Recitals 47-49; UN SDG 10; UN E-Gov Survey 2024
before.l1: No vulnerability assessment; citizen service AI does not identify or proactively support populations at risk of digital exclusion including elderly, disabled, homeless, or undocumented individuals
before.l3: Agent monitors service utilization patterns and identifies underserved groups, but does not implement proactive outreach or EU AI Act recital-aligned vulnerability protection
before.l5: Full vulnerability governance with EU AI Act recital-aligned vulnerable population identification, proactive service design for at-risk groups, UN SDG 10 equity monitoring, non-digital alternative channels, outreach to digitally excluded populations, and transparent equity reporting to oversight bodies

after.text: Is the agent prevented from exploiting the vulnerabilities of citizens due to age, disability or a specific social or economic situation to distort their behaviour in a way that causes or is likely to cause significant harm — for example nudging benefit claimants to withdraw or not pursue a claim (EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b))?
after.regulatoryRef: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) (applies from 2 Feb 2025)

after.l3: Policy forbids it and scripts are reviewed at launch, but changes to prompts or messages are not re-screened
after.l5: Every change to agent prompts, templates or messaging is screened against Art. 5(1)(b) before release, outcomes by vulnerable group are monitored for withdrawal or drop-off, and anomalies are investigated

citations.after: EU AI Act Art. 5(1)(b) (applies from 2 Feb 2025)

before.l5: Full UNCAC compliance with Art. 7 public sector integrity controls, Art. 9 procurement transparency, beneficial ownership verification, conflict of interest automated screening, bribery risk assessment in PPP activities, and anti-corruption audit trail per UNCAC Chapter IV

before.text: Does the agent implement UNCAC Article 9(1)(c) procurement transparency for PPP procurements by ensuring (1) pre-published tender rules and objective evaluation criteria, (2) traceable scoring and evaluation records for all bids, (3) publication of award rationales and conflict-of-interest declarations, (4) bidder debrief and complaint and appeal workflows, and (5) audit-ready evidence exports showing that AI-assisted recommendations did not override objective criteria?
before.l1: No Art. 9(1)(c) transparency: criteria are opaque, evaluation is not reproducible, and bidders have no defensible debrief and appeal evidence
before.l3: Some procurement artifacts exist (criteria, logs), but evaluation reproducibility, disclosure, and complaint handling are incomplete or not tied to AI-assisted steps
before.l5: Full Art. 9(1)(c) procurement transparency with objective criteria publication, reproducible evaluation trails, debrief and appeals, and AI decision traceability suitable for anti-corruption audit

after.text: Does the agent implement UNCAC Art. 9(1)(a)-(d) procurement transparency for PPP procurements by ensuring (1) public distribution of procurement information and award information, (2) conditions for participation and selection and award criteria set and published in advance, (3) objective and predetermined criteria applied with evaluation records that allow later verification, including where AI assisted, and (4) an effective domestic review and appeal route for bidders?
after.l1: Criteria are not published in advance, evaluation cannot be reproduced, and bidders have no review route
after.l3: Criteria and some evaluation logs exist, but AI-assisted scoring cannot be reproduced or the review route is not documented
after.l5: Published criteria before tender, reproducible evaluation records separating AI suggestions from evaluator decisions, published award information, and a documented review and appeal route with case outcomes

before.text: Does the agent implement OECD PPP Framework §5.1 value-for-money (VfM) by producing an ex ante lifecycle business case that includes (1) a public sector comparator (PSC) and counterfactual, (2) quantified risk allocation and risk-transfer valuation, (3) transparent discounting and demand and usage assumptions, (4) sensitivity and renegotiation scenario analysis, and (5) an evidence bundle (models, inputs, approvals) linking AI recommendations to the VfM rationale?
before.l1: No VfM discipline: decisions are made without a PSC and counterfactual, quantified risk valuation, or evidence linking recommendations to VfM
before.l3: Some cost-benefit work exists, but PSC, risk valuation, sensitivity and renegotiation analysis, and evidence bundles are incomplete
before.l5: Full §5.1 VfM implementation with PSC, risk valuation, sensitivity and renegotiation scenarios, and auditor-ready evidence packages for oversight review

after.text: Does the agent support PPP value-for-money decisions as the OECD PPP Recommendation sets out: a procurement option pre-test comparing lifetime costs of finance, construction and operation across delivery modes (Principle 5, Annex 5.1), a public sector comparator with a published methodology where relevant (Annex 5.2), and risk allocated to the party that can manage it at least cost (Principle 6, Annex 6.1), with an evidence bundle linking AI recommendations to the value-for-money rationale?
after.l1: Decisions are made without a pre-test, comparator or risk-allocation analysis
after.l3: A business case exists, but the comparator, risk allocation or the link from AI recommendations to the rationale is missing
after.l5: Pre-test, comparator with published methodology, risk-allocation matrix and sensitivity analysis on file per project, with AI recommendations traceable to each element

before.text: For PPP-related wire transfers (including cross-border payments), does the agent implement FATF Recommendation 16 by (1) capturing and validating originator and beneficiary information, (2) ensuring required information travels with the transfer through intermediaries, (3) screening against sanctions, PEP, and adverse media where applicable, (4) handling missing or invalid information with exception workflows, and (5) retaining audit evidence linking each payment to contract milestones and beneficial ownership data?
before.l1: No R16 controls: transfers lack required originator and beneficiary information integrity and cannot be traced end-to-end
before.l3: Captures payment metadata, but travel-rule style propagation, exception handling, screening, and audit linkage to PPP milestones are incomplete
before.l5: Full R16 compliance with validated originator and beneficiary data, propagation controls, screening plus exception workflows, and audit-ready traceability tying payments to PPP governance artifacts

before.text: Does the agent implement ISO 26000:2010 §6.6.7 anti-corruption by ensuring (1) anti-bribery and anti-corruption policy enforcement across partners, (2) third-party and intermediary due diligence, (3) gifts and hospitality and facilitation-payment controls, (4) whistleblowing and reporting intake with non-retaliation protections, and (5) auditable controls for political contributions and lobbying interactions in PPP contexts?
before.l1: No ISO 26000 anti-corruption program: anti-bribery controls are ad hoc and not consistently applied to partners and intermediaries
before.l3: Policies and some checks exist, but third-party due diligence, gifts and hospitality controls, reporting channels, and evidence retention are incomplete
before.l5: Full §6.6.7 anti-corruption implementation with partner-wide controls, due diligence, reporting mechanisms, and audit-ready evidence bundles

after.text: Does the agent support an anti-corruption programme across PPP partners and intermediaries — anti-bribery policy, third-party due diligence, gifts and hospitality controls, protected reporting channels, and records of political contributions and lobbying contacts — consistent with ISO 26000 clause 6.6.3 (anti-corruption) and the private-sector measures of UNCAC Art. 12?

after.l3: A policy exists and some partners are screened, but intermediary due diligence, reporting channels or records are incomplete
after.l5: Policy applied to every partner and intermediary, due diligence on file and refreshed on change, a protected reporting channel with case logs, and records of contributions and lobbying contacts

before.text: Does the agent implement G20 Responsible AI in Government §3 by ensuring AI-influenced PPP decisions (procurement shortlists, risk allocation recommendations, renegotiation triggers) have (1) documented rationale and explainability suitable for publication and oversight, (2) human accountability assignment, (3) contestability and appeal pathways for affected bidders and stakeholders, and (4) an auditable decision log separating AI suggestions from final human decisions?

before.l3: Some documentation exists, but explainability, contestability, and separation of AI suggestions from final decisions is inconsistent
before.l5: Full §3 operationalization with publishable rationales, human accountability, contestability workflows, and audit-ready logs of AI vs human decision steps

after.text: For AI-influenced PPP decisions (procurement shortlists, risk-allocation recommendations, renegotiation triggers), does the operator keep a decision log that separates AI suggestions from the final human decision, name the accountable official, publish a rationale suitable for oversight, and offer affected bidders a route to contest, consistent with the accountability principle of the OECD AI Recommendation and, where the system is high-risk, the deployer duties of EU AI Act Art. 26?
after.regulatoryRef: OECD AI Principles (accountability); EU AI Act Art. 26

after.l3: Officials are named, but the log does not separate AI suggestions from decisions or rationales are not published
after.l5: Decision log separating AI suggestion and human decision for every decision, named accountable official, published rationale, and a contest route with logged outcomes

citations.after: OECD AI Principles (accountability); EU AI Act Art. 26
